answer.text: Fungi steer carbon toward the seedlings most closely related to the donor
answer.line: Relatives come up once, in paragraph 14, as a payback evolution would need. No line says fungi steer carbon by kinship.

steps: Flip the job. Four choices have a line behind them; you are hunting the one that does not.
Check off four: mushrooms in paragraph 4, slow phosphate in paragraph 5, sugar made that week in paragraph 8, plants that make no sugar in paragraph 15.
Look hard at the one left. A relative appears only in paragraph 14, as one thing a donor would need back. A condition, not a finding.
Paragraph 13 even says flow may be set by the fungus, or simply by which end is hungrier.

choices.text: Some of the fungi that form mycorrhizas produce mushrooms on a forest floor
choices.note: Paragraph 4, sentence 4: many ectomycorrhizal fungi are the familiar mushrooms of forest floors.

choices.text: Fungi steer carbon toward the seedlings most closely related to the donor
choices.note: Kin appears only as a possible payback in paragraph 14. No line reports fungi routing carbon to relatives.

choices.text: Phosphate moves through soil slowly enough to leave a root short of it
choices.note: Paragraph 5: phosphate barely moves, so a root strips the soil around itself within days and sits in its own depletion zone.

choices.text: There are plants that live without making any sugar of their own
choices.note: Paragraph 15, sentence 2: ghost pipe and some orchids make no sugar at all. It sounds impossible for a plant, which is the pull.

choices.text: A share of what a tree makes in a given week ends up in fungal tissue
choices.note: Paragraph 8: part of a plant's output goes to its fungal partners, and the fungi live on sugar made that week.
